newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. says separate Rwandan fighters, refugees.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says separate Rwandan fighters, refugees.

text.p: A U.N. official on Wednesday called for weeding out militia from civilian refugees before any Rwandans in eastern Zaire return home.

Martin Griffith, the chief U.N. humanitarian coordinator in Central Africa, said repatriation would be difficult while fighting was going between ethnic Tutsi rebels and the government in eastern Zaire but detailed plans were being negotiated anyway.

If the refugees were on government territory, he said the armed radicals among them would have to be separated from others. If they were in areas controlled by the rebels, the separation would be done militarily and innocent people would be killed while the remainder would go back.
In either case, Griffiths said there would have to be some kind of international monitoring to ensure their safe return.

Among the refugees are members of the Hutu militia and former Rwandan government army responsible for the 1994 Rwanda genocide of more than 500,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus. They fled Rwanda to eastern Zaire, fearing revenge after the Tutsis fought their way into power in 1994.

Their control of teeming refugee camps has long been a sore point among internatinal aid groups, who have been criticised for maintaining them. Last autumn the rebel onslaught broke up most of the refugee camps, with the Hutu fighters often joining the Zairean government soldiers.
In Rwanda itself, the return of the refugees has endangered security in the western part of the country, with foreign aid workers and locals alike being killed.

"It would be very important if there is such a ceasefire as to where the refugees are at that time, whether in territory controlled by the alliance (rebels) or the Zaire administration," Griffiths, a Briton, told a news conference.

"This is because it is vital that there is a separation made between the refugees and the intimidators, who clearly contain a large measure of control, particularly of the Tingi Tingi populations," he said.

Most recently, fighting has forced some 200,000 of an estimated 370,000 Rwandans to move from their camps at Tingi-Tingi, Shabunda and Amisi in eastern Zaire. Up to 200,000 others remain unaccounted for.

"On the other hand if they end up in alliance territory, the alliance will of course no doubt proceed militarily to make that separation which will lead undoubtedly to a loss of lives among refugees," Griffiths added.

In Geneva, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees agency appealed to Zaire to reverse its decision to expel 40 aid workers it accused of precipitating an alleged slaughter by pulling out of the area.

UNHCR has attempted to negotiate security guarantees from the Kinshasa government and the rebels led by Laurent Kabila, whose forces are fighting to oust ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko. The rebels have captured a stretch of eastern Zaire bordering on Sudan, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi and Tanzania.
